story.title: Lindsay Clancy's Defense Challenges Evidence in Murder Case
story.summary: Lindsay Clancy returned to court for the first time since her murder trial ended in a mistrial. Her attorney argued that the prosecution failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove she killed her three children. This marks a significant shift in the defense's strategy, which previously focused on her mental state during the trial. A hearing has been set for November to discuss the possibility of a retrial.

explore_lenses.label: Why is the defense changing its argument now?
explore_lenses.title: The motion challenges proof, not only mental state
explore_lenses.summary: At trial, the defense centered on whether Clancy was criminally responsible because of mental illness. The new request asks Judge William Sullivan to find the prosecution’s evidence legally insufficient to establish that she committed the killings, which—if granted—would end the case without a retrial.

claims.text: During the first trial, defense attorney Kevin Reddington did not dispute that Clancy killed the children; the defense instead argued that postpartum psychosis meant she was not criminally responsible.

Reddington now argues that the case rests on speculation and that there was insufficient evidence that Clancy killed the children; he did not present an alternative account identifying another responsible person.
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called the new evidentiary argument “laughable,” while prosecutors maintain that trial evidence supported a conviction and that Clancy understood her actions were wrong.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: Judge Sullivan had not ruled on the defense request as of September 29, 2026.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case end in a mistrial?
explore_lenses.title: A deadlock left criminal responsibility unresolved
explore_lenses.summary: The mistrial did not resolve the charges or amount to an acquittal. Jurors failed to reach unanimity after hearing sharply conflicting accounts of Clancy’s mental condition and criminal responsibility at the time of the deaths.

claims.text: Judge Sullivan declared a mistrial on September 4, 2026, after seven days of deliberations; reporting on the September 29 hearing said the jury had been split 11-1 in Clancy’s favor on criminal responsibility.

The Commonwealth’s 2023 announcement said investigators developed probable cause and obtained an arrest warrant after first responders found the three children in the family home; a grand jury later indicted Clancy on murder charges.

The defense has also sought dismissal on double-jeopardy grounds, arguing that the court should have more fully investigated whether the sole holdout juror was following instructions on reasonable doubt before declaring a mistrial.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The court has not decided whether the mistrial procedure bars another prosecution, and the jurors’ deliberations themselves remain largely confidential.

explore_lenses.label: What will the November hearing decide?
explore_lenses.title: The court will address dismissal and a possible retrial
explore_lenses.summary: The next hearing is set for November 2, when the judge is expected to take up outstanding defense motions and require the parties to be ready to discuss scheduling if prosecutors pursue another trial. The prosecution has not yet committed publicly to retrying the case.

claims.text: Judge Sullivan set a November 2 hearing following the September 29 proceeding; it is expected to address whether the case should be retried and other defense motions, including dismissal and an inquiry concerning the holdout juror.

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said after the September 29 hearing that prosecutors had not yet decided whether to retry Clancy. AP reported options could include pursuing the existing first-degree murder charges, seeking lesser charges, or dropping the case.
Cruz said his office would do what it could “for the children,” while the defense seeks an acquittal or dismissal that would prevent a second trial.

story_report.summary: Lindsay Clancy returned to court after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, with her defense now arguing that prosecutors did not present sufficient evidence that she killed her three children. The argument differs from the first trial, when the defense did not dispute that Clancy caused the deaths and instead contended that postpartum psychosis left her not criminally responsible. Judge Sullivan scheduled a Nov. 2 hearing to consider a possible retrial and other defense motions.

sections.heading: Defense Challenges Evidence Against Clancy
sections.body: Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that the prosecution’s case rests on speculation and lacks evidence proving that Clancy killed the children. He did not offer an alternative account identifying another person as responsible. Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called the new argument “laughable,” and prosecutors maintain that the evidence supported conviction and showed that Clancy understood her actions were wrong.

sections.heading: Mistrial Procedure Draws Defense Challenge
sections.body: Judge Sullivan declared a mistrial Sept. 4, 2026, after seven days of deliberations. Reporting on the later court hearing said the jury was split 11-1 in Clancy’s favor on criminal responsibility. The defense has separately sought dismissal on double-jeopardy grounds, arguing that the court should have further examined whether the lone holdout juror was applying the reasonable-doubt instruction before the mistrial was declared.

sections.heading: Prosecutors Weigh Future Clancy Case
sections.body: The Nov. 2 hearing is expected to address whether the case should be retried, along with defense requests for dismissal and an inquiry involving the holdout juror. Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said prosecutors had not yet decided whether to retry Clancy. Reported options include pursuing the existing first-degree murder charges, seeking lesser charges or dropping the case, while the defense seeks an acquittal or dismissal that would prevent another trial.

related_stories.title: Tu-95 Bomber Crash in Far East Claims Six Lives
related_stories.summary: A Russian Tu-95 bomber crashed during a training flight in the Amur region, resulting in the deaths of six crew members. The incident occurred shortly after takeoff from the Ukrainka air base, which had been used to shelter aircraft following significant damage from Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb in June 2025.
